lines.text: Learn streaming in small steps

First understand an event, its key, where it is stored and when a consumer records progress. Then run the small supplied fixture and one failure/replay exercise. Complete the M14 lessons and G05 requirements in order; you do not need to add production cluster administration, certification preparation or a multi-region Kafka deployment. Keep those as later specialization when your work needs them.
M14 lesson 1 of 12 | Primary practice: practice/kafka/01_* and simulator evidence where supplied
Why this matters
Most data engineers already understand batch because M08-M13 repeatedly used bounded files or
tables. Streaming changes one assumption: there may be no natural 'all rows are here' moment.
That affects when you compute, how you recover, and what 'done' means. Interviewers use this topic
to see whether you can reason about continuous data rather than merely repeat that streaming is
faster.
Picture it in your head
Picture a mandi truck register. A batch workflow is the clerk collecting all slips until 10 PM and then
entering them together. A streaming workflow is each truck crossing the gate and creating an event
immediately. The business can react sooner, but now the system must tolerate events arriving
forever, late, duplicated, or temporarily out of order.
New words before use

rows: One immutable statement that something happened, normally with a key, value and timestamp.
A finite input with a known end, such as one daily file.
A logical input that can continue producing events indefinitely.
Time between an event happening and the useful result becoming available.
Amount of data processed per unit time.
A streaming engine execution style that processes small bounded chunks repeatedly.

lines.text: Useful video / source route
VIDEO: Confluent Developer - Stream Processing | Apache Kafka 101 (2025 Edition)
Verified chapters 00:00-04:10: stream processing and batch/stream comparison
OFFICIAL/CURRENT: Official Spark 4.2 Structured Streaming + Kafka integration
Current Kafka source/sink, options and deployment package
Use rule: videos are strongly encouraged for visual learning, but the learner book + supplied practice are
self-sufficient. If a video is older or vendor-specific, use it for the concept/visual and use current official
docs for version-sensitive commands.
Follow with me once
A courier company receives parcel scans. In the batch design, 60,000 scans land as one hourly file.
In the streaming design, each scan is emitted when the barcode is read. If fraud/routing alerts can
wait an hour, batch may be simpler and cheaper. If a misrouted parcel must be stopped before the
truck leaves, the value of low latency can justify Kafka and streaming complexity. The key
engineering decision is not 'streaming is modern'; it is whether business latency, replay and
continuous availability requirements justify the operational cost.
What you should see
You should be able to classify a workload by bounded/unbounded input, required response time,
replay need and failure tolerance. You should also be able to say that Spark Structured Streaming
usually executes continuous logic as repeated micro-batches even though the logical input is
unbounded.
Why it worked
The result follows from the contract just introduced rather than from a memorized command.
Preserve the evidence that proves the contract: keys/partitions/offsets, committed positions, sink
reconciliation, checkpoint state or lag by partition as appropriate.
Break it / common failure
A common beginner mistake is treating streaming as 'batch every second'. That misses persistent
offsets, long-running consumer state, backpressure/lag and restart behavior. Another mistake is
selecting Kafka because the source updates frequently even when the business only needs a daily
result.
Reason through a realistic incident
An operations dashboard is 25 minutes behind. The producer is healthy and events are durable in
Kafka. Is this data loss? Not necessarily. First separate event-time freshness from consumer
progress: inspect the newest produced offset/timestamp, the consumer group's committed position
and processing rate. Growing lag is a capacity or failure symptom, not proof that events
disappeared.
Deepen the engineering reasoning
The important design move is to separate arrival cadence from decision cadence. Data may arrive
every second while one consumer reacts instantly, another publishes five-minute operational
summaries, and finance still closes a daily batch. Streaming therefore does not mean every
calculation must run record-by-record forever. It means the system can observe an unbounded
sequence and update work as new records arrive. Batch does not mean old-fashioned or inferior; a
bounded input can be easier to reconcile, rerun and approve. When you design a pipeline, write the
business latency target first: for example, alert within 10 seconds, dashboard within 5 minutes,
settlement by 02:00. Then choose the simplest execution model that meets each target. Also name
the recovery boundary. A continuously running job still needs durable source history or
checkpoint/state evidence so a crash does not turn into silent data loss. The engineering goal is not
'real time everywhere'; it is correct enough, soon enough, with a recoverable history.
Now you do a changed version alone
For three cases - nightly payroll, parcel-location alerting, and a daily regulatory archive - choose
batch, streaming, or a hybrid. For each, state the tolerated latency and the replay/recovery
expectation.
Fresh changed retry
Change parcel alerting so the customer app may be 10 minutes late but the fraud engine must react
in under 3 seconds. Explain why one event stream can feed consumers with different latency
requirements.
Validation and recovery ladder
•  First prove the broker/source is reachable before changing application logic.
•  Name the topic, partition, key/group/query identity and the exact progress marker you are relying
on.
•  Reconcile input evidence against valid output + quarantine/error outcomes; do not use a green
process as proof of correctness.
•  If a failure can cause replay, prove the sink or side effect handles replay safely before you call the
pipeline reliable.
•  Keep the genuine first attempt/error. A corrected run is repair evidence; the changed retry proves
mastery.
Ready-made revision
Streaming is not chosen because it is fashionable. Choose it when continuous arrival plus
latency/replay requirements justify persistent consumer state and operational complexity.
Evidence / mastery
Save: command or code used, one expected output, one failure/recovery note, and one sentence
explaining the guarantee/boundary in your own words. You are ready only when you can solve the
changed retry with the review closed.
M14 lesson 2 of 12 | Primary practice: practice/kafka/02_* and simulator evidence where supplied
Why this matters
Everything else in Kafka depends on a precise mental model of where an event goes. If you confuse
a topic with a database table, or a broker with a consumer, later reasoning about partitions, retention
and lag becomes fragile.
Picture it in your head
Think of a topic as a named, append-only stream of envelopes. Each broker is one warehouse
machine that stores pieces of those streams. Producers deliver envelopes to the cluster; consumers
read them without removing them. Kafka keeps events according to retention rules, so one
consumer reading does not make the event vanish for another consumer.
New words before use

rows: A Kafka server that stores topic partitions and serves client requests.
A set of Kafka brokers operating as one logical service.
A named append-only stream/log of events.
A key, value and metadata such as timestamp and headers.
The rule controlling how long or how much log data Kafka keeps.
Kafka's built-in metadata/controller architecture; the current route does not use ZooKeeper.

VIDEO: Confluent Developer - Topics | Apache Kafka 101 (2025 Edition)
Verified chapters 00:00-09:50: log abstraction, messages, timestamps, retention
VIDEO: Confluent Developer - Brokers | Apache Kafka 101 (2025 Edition)
Verified chapters 00:00-03:12: brokers, clusters and KRaft
OFFICIAL/CURRENT: Official Apache Kafka Quickstart
Current 4.3.1 local/KRaft/Docker commands
Use rule: videos are strongly encouraged for visual learning, but the learner book + supplied practice are
self-sufficient. If a video is older or vendor-specific, use it for the concept/visual and use current official
docs for version-sensitive commands.
Follow with me once
Start the official apache/kafka:4.3.1 container and create a topic called parcel-status. Produce three
lines and consume them from the beginning. Then run a second consumer from the beginning. The
same stored records are still available because consumption does not delete them. This is the first
major difference from a simple work queue mental model.
docker exec m14-kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh --create --topic parcel-status --bootstrap-server localhost
docker exec -it m14-kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-console-producer.sh --topic parcel-status --bootstrap-server loca
docker exec -it m14-kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-console-consumer.sh --topic parcel-status --from-beginning --boot
What you should see
A topic description should show at least one partition and leader. The console consumer should print
the produced records. Re-running a consumer with an explicit from-beginning route can read
retained records again.
Why it worked
The result follows from the contract just introduced rather than from a memorized command.
Preserve the evidence that proves the contract: keys/partitions/offsets, committed positions, sink
reconciliation, checkpoint state or lag by partition as appropriate.
Break it / common failure
If the client cannot connect, distinguish 'container not running' from 'topic missing' from 'listener/port
wrong'. Do not randomly change ports. First prove docker ps shows the broker, then list topics with
the broker-local CLI, then test the host port.
Reason through a realistic incident
A team says yesterday's events are gone because their new consumer starts and sees only fresh
traffic. Before blaming retention, check the consumer starting position and group state. A new group
with auto.offset.reset=latest may begin at the end; that is different from the broker deleting history.
Deepen the engineering reasoning
A Kafka topic becomes easier to reason about when you stop picturing it as a mailbox that empties.
Records are appended to partition logs and remain available according to retention policy. A
consumer group stores its own progress separately, so two applications can read the same topic
independently. That separation is why one stream can support fraud detection, analytics and auditing
without copying the producer three times. Retention is therefore not cosmetic configuration: it sets a
replay horizon. If the topic keeps seven days but your incident is discovered on day ten, the group
offset alone cannot recover deleted records; you need another durable raw/archive source. Topic
design also needs a business boundary. A topic named everything-events gives flexibility at first but
often creates unclear ownership, schemas and retention. Prefer a topic whose event family, owners
and contract can be stated. Finally, brokers host partitions and replicas, while the topic is the logical
name. KRaft is the current Kafka coordination architecture in this course; ZooKeeper-era tutorials
can still explain concepts, but they are not the setup authority.
Now you do a changed version alone
Create three domain topic names for an e-commerce system. For each, write one sentence
describing what a single event means and what retention purpose the topic serves.
Fresh changed retry
Change the parcel-status topic from a transient dashboard feed to an audit source that must support
seven-day replay. Explain which topic-level policy becomes more important and why consumers still
need their own offsets.
Validation and recovery ladder
•  First prove the broker/source is reachable before changing application logic.
•  Name the topic, partition, key/group/query identity and the exact progress marker you are relying
on.
•  Reconcile input evidence against valid output + quarantine/error outcomes; do not use a green
process as proof of correctness.
•  If a failure can cause replay, prove the sink or side effect handles replay safely before you call the
pipeline reliable.
•  Keep the genuine first attempt/error. A corrected run is repair evidence; the changed retry proves
mastery.
Ready-made revision
Topics store retained events; brokers host partitions; consumers do not delete records when they
read them. Kafka 4.x uses KRaft-era architecture, not ZooKeeper in this course.
Evidence / mastery
Save: command or code used, one expected output, one failure/recovery note, and one sentence
explaining the guarantee/boundary in your own words. You are ready only when you can solve the
changed retry with the review closed.
M14 lesson 3 of 12 | Primary practice: practice/kafka/03_* and simulator evidence where supplied
Why this matters
A producer is not merely 'send JSON'. Producer choices decide durability, partition placement and
therefore ordering/scalability. Message keys are especially important because they connect business
identity to partition-level ordering.
Picture it in your head
Imagine several parcel conveyor belts. The topic is the whole conveyor system; partitions are
individual belts. A message key acts like a routing label. If all events for parcel P17 use the same
stable key, the partitioner can keep those events on one belt, which makes per-parcel order
tractable. If the key changes randomly, related events can scatter.
New words before use

rows: Client that publishes events to Kafka.
Optional bytes used by partitioning logic and downstream semantics.
Logic that chooses a partition when one is not explicitly supplied.
Function invoked when an asynchronous produce succeeds or permanently fails.
Producer mode that prevents duplicates caused by retrying the same producer sequence under supported conditions.

OFFICIAL/CURRENT: Official Apache Kafka Producer Configs
Current acks/idempotence/retry behavior
Use rule: videos are strongly encouraged for visual learning, but the learner book + supplied practice are
self-sufficient. If a video is older or vendor-specific, use it for the concept/visual and use current official
docs for version-sensitive commands.
Follow with me once
Publish shipment events keyed by shipment_id. Send SHP-42 CREATED, SHP-42 LOADED and
SHP-42 DEPARTED using the same key, while other shipments use their own keys. Observe the
delivery callback partition and offset. You are not trying to memorize a hash algorithm; you are
proving that a stable key creates a stable routing intent and that delivery success must be observed
rather than assumed when produce() returns.
What you should see
Each callback should identify a topic/partition/offset or an error. Repeated events with the same key
should be routed consistently by a stable partitioner while the partition count is unchanged. Do not
promise a partition number across a partition-count change.
Why it worked
The result follows from the contract just introduced rather than from a memorized command.
Preserve the evidence that proves the contract: keys/partitions/offsets, committed positions, sink
reconciliation, checkpoint state or lag by partition as appropriate.
Break it / common failure
Two dangerous beginner habits are ignoring delivery callbacks and using a random UUID as the key
for every event. The first hides failed delivery; the second destroys useful grouping. Also do not
hard-code a partition unless you own the operational consequences.
Reason through a realistic incident
A customer's status appears as DELIVERED before OUT_FOR_DELIVERY in a downstream
service. Before blaming Kafka, ask whether both events had the same key and therefore the same
partition. Kafka guarantees order within a partition, not global topic order across partitions.
Deepen the engineering reasoning
A key solves two related but different problems: routing and business grouping. If order_id is the key,
all events for one order can be routed consistently while the partition count and partitioner behavior
remain stable. That supports per-order ordering, but it does not mean every order in the topic is
globally ordered relative to every other order. Write the sentence 'I need order within X' before
choosing the key. Durability is a separate axis. The producer may accept a record into its local buffer
before the broker has acknowledged it; delivery callbacks or equivalent delivery evidence tell you
whether the record eventually reached the broker or failed. Current producer idempotence reduces
some retry-duplicate risks, but it does not turn two separate calls carrying the same business event
into one logical event. Your event contract still benefits from a stable event_id. In a design review
ask: what key is used, what order does that promise, what happens if the key is hot, and what
evidence proves delivery rather than merely enqueueing work locally?
Now you do a changed version alone
Design keys for order-events, customer-profile-changes and device-temperature. State what
ordering you need and one hotspot/skew risk for each key.
Fresh changed retry
Assume one enterprise customer produces 40% of all events under one customer_id key. Keep
per-order ordering while reducing hotspot risk by changing the key design to a finer business entity.
Validation and recovery ladder
•  First prove the broker/source is reachable before changing application logic.
•  Name the topic, partition, key/group/query identity and the exact progress marker you are relying
on.
•  Reconcile input evidence against valid output + quarantine/error outcomes; do not use a green
process as proof of correctness.
•  If a failure can cause replay, prove the sink or side effect handles replay safely before you call the
pipeline reliable.
•  Keep the genuine first attempt/error. A corrected run is repair evidence; the changed retry proves
mastery.
Ready-made revision
Use keys to express the unit whose order/grouping matters. Producer durability and delivery
confirmation are separate from business-level deduplication downstream.
Evidence / mastery
Save: command or code used, one expected output, one failure/recovery note, and one sentence
explaining the guarantee/boundary in your own words. You are ready only when you can solve the
changed retry with the review closed.
M14 lesson 4 of 12 | Primary practice: practice/kafka/04_* and simulator evidence where supplied
Why this matters
Most streaming correctness bugs happen after an event is read: code performs a side effect,
crashes, and then either loses or repeats work depending on when it committed progress. A safe
consumer therefore needs a processing contract, not just a poll loop.
Picture it in your head
A consumer is a clerk reading numbered pages from a durable log. The clerk can bookmark
progress with an offset commit. If the bookmark is moved before the page is actually processed, a
crash can skip work. If the bookmark moves after durable work, a crash can repeat a page - so the
side effect must tolerate replay.
New words before use

rows: Ask the broker/client library for available records and background events.
Persist a consumer group position for a partition.
Client-managed periodic offset commit; convenient but easy to misunderstand.
Application-controlled commit after a chosen processing boundary.
External durable action such as database write, file append or API call.
Record that repeatedly fails validation/processing and can block progress without a policy.

VIDEO: Confluent Developer - Consumers | Apache Kafka 101 (2025 Edition)
Verified chapters: 01:13-05:04 subscription/records/log; 05:04-06:31 commits; 06:31-08:04
groups/rebalancing
VIDEO: Confluent Developer - What is a Kafka Consumer and How does it work?
Optional visual - no verified bounded range; 6-minute consumer overview
OFFICIAL/CURRENT: Official Apache Kafka Consumer Configs
Current group/offset/commit client configuration
Use rule: videos are strongly encouraged for visual learning, but the learner book + supplied practice are
self-sufficient. If a video is older or vendor-specific, use it for the concept/visual and use current official
docs for version-sensitive commands.
Follow with me once
Use a consumer with enable.auto.commit=False. For each parcel event: decode JSON, validate
required fields, write/upsert to a local durable sink using event_id as a uniqueness key, then
synchronously commit that message's offset. If validation fails, save the raw event and reason to a
quarantine file instead of silently committing as success. The exact production retry/DLQ architecture
can vary, but the ordering of 'durable outcome before progress commit' is the important reasoning
pattern.
What you should see
After a clean run, the sink contains one durable row per event_id and the group has a committed
position beyond processed records. If the process is killed after the sink write but before the commit,
replay may happen; the idempotent sink prevents a duplicate business effect.
Why it worked
The result follows from the contract just introduced rather than from a memorized command.
Preserve the evidence that proves the contract: keys/partitions/offsets, committed positions, sink
reconciliation, checkpoint state or lag by partition as appropriate.
Break it / common failure
Committing first is the classic loss window. Writing an external API/database and assuming Kafka
transactions cover that external side effect is another mistake. Kafka's own transactional guarantees
do not magically make arbitrary third-party systems transactional.
Reason through a realistic incident
A payment consumer restarted and sent one email twice. The event existed once in Kafka. That can
still happen: the email side effect succeeded, the process died before progress was safely recorded,
and the event replayed. Fix the side-effect contract or deduplication, not the event log.
Deepen the engineering reasoning
The safest consumer design names a handled outcome for every record. A valid record may create
or upsert a durable business row. An invalid record may be durably quarantined with the raw bytes,
topic, partition, offset and failure reason. Only after one of those outcomes is durable should the
application advance committed progress under the chosen policy. That is why the supplied
consumer persists quarantine evidence before committing a poison record: logging 'bad record' to
the console is not durable handling. This still does not create universal exactly-once behavior. If the
valid path calls an external payment or email API, a crash can occur after the remote side effect
succeeds but before the Kafka progress commit. Replaying the event is correct from Kafka's
perspective, but the external effect may repeat unless it accepts an idempotency key or you
coordinate work through a durable outbox/state table. The useful mental model is: Kafka controls
read progress; your application owns the side-effect contract. Test the crash window deliberately
rather than assuming a happy-path run proves correctness.
Now you do a changed version alone
Write the safe order of operations for a consumer that writes to PostgreSQL. Include validation,
durable write, reconciliation evidence and offset commit.
Fresh changed retry
Change the sink to a non-idempotent REST API. Explain why the same offset strategy is no longer
sufficient and propose an outbox/idempotency-key or durable work-state approach.
Validation and recovery ladder
•  First prove the broker/source is reachable before changing application logic.
•  Name the topic, partition, key/group/query identity and the exact progress marker you are relying
on.
•  Reconcile input evidence against valid output + quarantine/error outcomes; do not use a green
process as proof of correctness.
•  If a failure can cause replay, prove the sink or side effect handles replay safely before you call the
pipeline reliable.
•  Keep the genuine first attempt/error. A corrected run is repair evidence; the changed retry proves
mastery.
Ready-made revision
Consumer correctness is the relationship between processing, durable side effects and committed
offsets. Prefer replay-safe work over pretending replay never happens.
Evidence / mastery
Save: command or code used, one expected output, one failure/recovery note, and one sentence
explaining the guarantee/boundary in your own words. You are ready only when you can solve the
changed retry with the review closed.
Trace the commit decision

For malformed input, preserve the raw event and a rejection reason durably, then commit that Kafka message. For a valid event, write the business ledger durably, then commit. If the valid write fails, propagate the error and do not commit or relabel it as bad source data. A commit failure after a successful ledger write can cause replay. Identical event_id and payload then becomes a no-op; changed payload under that ID is a conflict requiring investigation.
M14 lesson 5 of 12 | Primary practice: practice/kafka/05_* and simulator evidence where supplied
Why this matters
Partitions give Kafka parallelism and scale, but they also define the boundary of ordering. This
trade-off appears constantly in interviews and production incidents.
Picture it in your head
A topic with four partitions is four ordered notebooks, not one globally ordered notebook. Each
notebook has its own offsets 0,1,2... Reading all notebooks together can interleave events in many
valid ways. The only strict order you can rely on is inside one partition.
New words before use

rows: Ordered append-only sub-log within a topic.
Business key whose records should route consistently.
One total order across all events - Kafka partitions do not provide this by default.
Uneven distribution of events/work across partitions.
Number of parallel sub-logs; changing it can change future key routing.

lines.text: Useful video / source route
VIDEO: Confluent Developer - Partitions | Apache Kafka 101 (2025 Edition)
Verified chapters 00:41-03:23: scaling and partition ordering
VIDEO: Confluent Developer - Topics | Apache Kafka 101 (2025 Edition)
Verified chapters 00:00-09:50: log abstraction, messages, timestamps, retention
Use rule: videos are strongly encouraged for visual learning, but the learner book + supplied practice are
self-sufficient. If a video is older or vendor-specific, use it for the concept/visual and use current official
docs for version-sensitive commands.
Follow with me once
Take 12 events for four shipments. Route each shipment consistently to one simulated partition, then
print offsets per partition. You will see order preserved for SHP-1 inside its partition even though
events from SHP-1 and SHP-2 interleave when viewed across the topic. Next simulate one key
producing eight of the twelve events and observe hotspot risk.
What you should see
You should be able to reconstruct each business entity's local order from its partition sequence. You
should not claim the combined topic has a single meaningful order unless the topic has one partition
or the application builds another ordering mechanism.
Why it worked
The result follows from the contract just introduced rather than from a memorized command.
Preserve the evidence that proves the contract: keys/partitions/offsets, committed positions, sink
reconciliation, checkpoint state or lag by partition as appropriate.
Break it / common failure
Increasing partitions after designing 'hash(key) -> partition' can move future records for the same
key, depending on the partitioner. Also, choosing customer_id as a key may preserve customer
order but create a hotspot for a huge customer. Key design is a business and distribution decision
together.
Reason through a realistic incident
Only partition 2 has rising lag while partitions 0,1,3 are healthy. This is a clue: inspect key distribution
and slow records for that partition. Scaling consumers cannot overcome a single hot partition if only
one consumer can actively process that partition in the group at a time.
Deepen the engineering reasoning
Partition count is both a scalability choice and a correctness boundary. A consumer group can
process different partitions in parallel, while each partition remains ordered. Six partitions can
therefore provide up to six active partition assignments in a group at one moment, but useful
throughput is still constrained by record cost, broker capacity, downstream sinks and skew. More
partitions are not free: they add metadata, open files, leader/replica work and more ordering
boundaries. Key distribution matters just as much as count. A single hot key stays on one partition,
so adding consumers can leave the bottleneck unchanged while other consumers sit idle. When a
dashboard shows events 'out of order,' first compare topic, partition and offset for the related
business entity. If the events are in different partitions, Kafka may have preserved every local log
perfectly while the merged display interleaves them. If strict global order is truly required, one
partition is the simplest boundary but sacrifices parallelism. Most real systems narrow the required
order to an entity such as order_id, device_id or account_id.
Now you do a changed version alone
For a food-delivery stream choose a key for driver-location, restaurant-order and payment-event
topics. State exactly which order each choice preserves.
Fresh changed retry
A marketplace has one seller generating 50% of orders. Redesign a seller_id-keyed topic so
order-level processing scales while seller-level totals can still be computed downstream.
Validation and recovery ladder
•  First prove the broker/source is reachable before changing application logic.
•  Name the topic, partition, key/group/query identity and the exact progress marker you are relying
on.
•  Reconcile input evidence against valid output + quarantine/error outcomes; do not use a green
process as proof of correctness.
•  If a failure can cause replay, prove the sink or side effect handles replay safely before you call the
pipeline reliable.
•  Keep the genuine first attempt/error. A corrected run is repair evidence; the changed retry proves
mastery.
Ready-made revision
Partitions are the unit of parallelism and ordered log storage. Preserve the order that matters by
keying related events together, then watch for skew.
Evidence / mastery
Save: command or code used, one expected output, one failure/recovery note, and one sentence
explaining the guarantee/boundary in your own words. You are ready only when you can solve the
changed retry with the review closed.
M14 lesson 6 of 12 | Primary practice: practice/kafka/06_* and simulator evidence where supplied
Why this matters
Offsets make Kafka replayable. They let a consumer group say 'this is how far I have safely
progressed' without deleting the underlying events. Understanding offsets is what separates Kafka
from a simple queue mental model.
Picture it in your head
Each partition is a book with numbered lines. The offset is the line number, not a business ID. A
consumer group's committed offset is a bookmark. Resetting or seeking changes the bookmark; it
does not rewrite the book.
New words before use

rows: Monotonic position of a record within one partition.
Stored group progress used after restart/reassignment.
Common reset policies when a valid committed position is absent.
Read retained events again from an earlier position.
Explicitly change the position from which a consumer reads.
Old data may no longer exist if the topic has already deleted it.

VIDEO: Confluent Developer - Consumers | Apache Kafka 101 (2025 Edition)
Verified chapters: 01:13-05:04 subscription/records/log; 05:04-06:31 commits; 06:31-08:04
groups/rebalancing
OFFICIAL/CURRENT: Official Kafka distribution - consumer offset tracking
How committed offsets are stored and recovered
OFFICIAL/CURRENT: Official Apache Kafka Consumer Configs
Current group/offset/commit client configuration
Use rule: videos are strongly encouraged for visual learning, but the learner book + supplied practice are
self-sufficient. If a video is older or vendor-specific, use it for the concept/visual and use current official
docs for version-sensitive commands.
Follow with me once
Consume five events and commit after event 5. Produce three more. Restart the same group: it
should resume after the committed position. Then use a new group or explicit reset route to read
earlier retained events. This proves that group position and topic storage are separate concepts.
What you should see
Same group + valid commit resumes from its recorded positions. New group behavior depends on
reset policy. Replay works only while the required offsets still exist under retention.
Why it worked
The result follows from the contract just introduced rather than from a memorized command.
Preserve the evidence that proves the contract: keys/partitions/offsets, committed positions, sink
reconciliation, checkpoint state or lag by partition as appropriate.
Break it / common failure
auto.offset.reset does not normally override an existing valid committed offset. Another common
mistake is saying 'offset 50' without naming the partition; offsets are partition-local.
Reason through a realistic incident
A bug corrupted derived rows between noon and 12:20. You fix the code and want to replay. First
identify the source partitions and time/offset boundary, preserve existing evidence, and ensure the
sink is idempotent or is rebuilt in an isolated target. Blindly rewinding a production group can
duplicate external effects.
Deepen the engineering reasoning
Offsets are mechanical positions, not business timestamps or IDs. Partition 0 offset 25 and partition
1 offset 25 are unrelated positions in different logs. A consumer group's committed offsets describe
restart progress, while the broker's log-end offsets describe how far each partition has advanced.
Their difference is one form of lag. Replay is therefore a controlled change in read position, not a
mutation of Kafka history. A common beginner mistake is setting auto.offset.reset=earliest on an
existing group and expecting it to reread everything. That policy is consulted when the group has no
valid committed position for a partition; an existing valid commit normally wins. A safe replay plan
names the exact partitions and range, retention availability, destination/sink isolation, idempotency

Why this matters
Consumer groups are how Kafka parallelizes one logical application while allowing completely
separate applications to read the same topic independently. Misunderstanding this leads to both
under-scaling and duplicate business work.
Picture it in your head

partitions among them, so each partition has one active worker in that group. A second team with a
different badge can read the same six partitions independently.

Follow with me once
Model a topic with six partitions. With one consumer, it owns all six. With two, assignments split. With
six, each can own one. With eight, two have no partition work for that topic. Then create analytics-v1
and email-v1 as different group IDs: each group receives the full topic independently.
What you should see
You should be able to predict whether adding consumers increases parallelism and whether two
consumers will share work or each receive all events based on group.id.
Why it worked
The result follows from the contract just introduced rather than from a memorized command.
Preserve the evidence that proves the contract: keys/partitions/offsets, committed positions, sink
reconciliation, checkpoint state or lag by partition as appropriate.
Break it / common failure
Starting every replica with a random group.id creates independent readers and can multiply side
effects. Starting unrelated applications with the same group.id makes them accidentally share work.
Both bugs look like 'Kafka randomly lost/duplicated messages' until group identity is inspected.
Reason through a realistic incident
A deployment doubles replicas from 3 to 8, but throughput barely changes on a 3-partition topic. That
is expected: normal group parallelism is partition-bounded. Either processing per partition must get
faster or partitioning must be reconsidered with key/order consequences.
Deepen the engineering reasoning
A consumer group is an application-level collaboration boundary. Consumers with the same group.id
divide the group's assigned partitions; consumers with different group IDs are independent
subscriptions and may each process every retained record. That distinction is how one topic can
feed both fraud and analytics. Scaling a group depends on partition count: if a topic has six partitions,
ten healthy consumers in one group cannot all own a partition simultaneously in the ordinary model.
Four may remain idle, though they can help after failures or rebalances. Rebalancing is not merely a
harmless control-plane detail. If consumers join or leave repeatedly, or processing blocks
polling/heartbeats, partitions may move and work may pause. Records near the handoff can replay
depending on commit timing. An incident timeline should therefore record assignment changes,
poll/processing latency and commit positions. Before 'add more consumers,' determine whether the
bottleneck is lack of parallel partitions, one hot partition, slow downstream I/O, excessive rebalance
churn or expensive record processing. Scaling the wrong layer adds complexity without fixing
throughput.

Why this matters
'Exactly once' is one of the most abused phrases in data engineering. You need to separate
producer duplicate prevention, Kafka transactions, consumer offset behavior and external side
effects. Correct answers state the boundary of the guarantee.
Picture it in your head
Think of a bank transfer request crossing several checkpoints. Preventing the Kafka producer from
appending the same retry twice is one boundary. Atomically writing Kafka output and Kafka offsets is
another. Calling a bank API or inserting into a separate database is outside that Kafka transaction
unless you design an additional idempotency/transaction pattern.

Follow with me once
Simulate an order-status consumer. Run 1 writes order O9=PAID, crashes before its progress
commit, and run 2 replays the same event. An append-only sink now has two rows; an upsert keyed
by event_id or order/version has one final effect. Then contrast this with Kafka producer
idempotence: it protects producer retry duplicates, but it does not automatically deduplicate two
intentionally produced business events with different identities.
What you should see
You should be able to draw a boundary around what Kafka's idempotent producer/transactions
protect and what still requires application or sink idempotency. Current Kafka producer idempotence
is enabled by default when no conflicting configs disable it; acks=all is part of the compatible setting
set.
Why it worked
The result follows from the contract just introduced rather than from a memorized command.
Preserve the evidence that proves the contract: keys/partitions/offsets, committed positions, sink
reconciliation, checkpoint state or lag by partition as appropriate.
Break it / common failure
Saying 'Kafka guarantees exactly once end to end' without naming source, processor and sink is
unsafe. Another mistake is using payload equality as deduplication identity; two legitimate
identical-valued events can exist.
Reason through a realistic incident
A consumer writes to a payment database and then commits its offset. It crashes after the DB
commit. On restart the event is replayed. A Kafka transaction cannot roll back the external DB
commit. Use a business idempotency key, transactional outbox/inbox, or equivalent durable
coordination pattern.
Deepen the engineering reasoning
Delivery guarantees must always name their boundary. Producer idempotence is about preventing
duplicate records caused by certain producer retry sequences; it is not a business deduplication
service for two intentionally submitted events. Kafka transactions can atomically coordinate Kafka
records and consumed offsets for supported Kafka-to-Kafka workflows, but an external database,
email provider or payment API is outside that transaction unless you add another coordination
mechanism. This is why 'exactly once' is incomplete by itself. Ask: exactly once where, and for which
effect? For an external sink, a stable event_id plus a uniqueness constraint/upsert, an idempotency
key accepted by the API, or a transactional outbox/inbox can convert replay into a harmless repeat.
Separate duplicate records from duplicate business effects. A topic might contain the same event
twice yet an idempotent sink applies one effect; conversely one Kafka record can trigger two emails
if application logic retries incorrectly. Evidence should therefore include both transport metadata and
sink/business reconciliation.

event_id/idempotency-key mapping and evidence you would save.

pipeline reliable.
•  Keep the genuine first attempt/error. A corrected run is repair evidence; the changed retry proves
mastery.
Ready-made revision
Guarantees are scoped. Producer idempotence handles producer retries; replay-safe
consumers/sinks handle external effects; Kafka transactions cover Kafka-managed atomic
boundaries, not arbitrary external systems.

M14 lesson 9 of 12 | Primary practice: practice/kafka/09_* and simulator evidence where supplied
Why this matters
Kafka stores keys and values as bytes. Teams still need a contract that says what those bytes mean.
Without schema discipline, a producer can make a harmless-looking field change that breaks many
consumers at once.
Picture it in your head
A schema is the label and shape printed on a shipping form. Serialization turns the structured form
into bytes for transport; deserialization reconstructs it. Schema evolution is changing the form while
old and new readers may coexist.
New words before use

currency with a safe default. A v1 event can still be interpreted by a reader that understands v2.
Contrast that with renaming order_id to id without a compatibility strategy: consumers expecting

What you should see

rename/type changes, while acknowledging exact compatibility rules depend on Avro/Protobuf/JSON
Schema and registry configuration.
Why it worked
The result follows from the contract just introduced rather than from a memorized command.
Preserve the evidence that proves the contract: keys/partitions/offsets, committed positions, sink
reconciliation, checkpoint state or lag by partition as appropriate.
Break it / common failure
'JSON is self-describing so we do not need schemas' is a weak production argument. JSON syntax
tells you that a field exists, not whether a business contract permits it, whether it is required, or
whether changing its type is compatible.
Reason through a realistic incident
A producer changes amount from numeric 19.99 to string '19.99 INR'. Some consumers silently cast;
others fail. The real problem is contract evolution without controlled compatibility. Restore/introduce
a schema boundary and change representation through an explicit versioned migration.
Deepen the engineering reasoning
Serialization answers 'how are these bytes interpreted?' while a schema answers 'what fields, types
and constraints does this event promise?' A schema registry adds shared contract/version
management, but compatibility is never just 'old versus new looks similar.' It depends on the
serialization format and configured compatibility policy. A practical evolution plan distinguishes
additive from destructive change. Adding an optional currency field while older consumers still read
order_id and amount can often be introduced safely under an appropriate compatibility policy.
Renaming order_id to id, changing amount from numeric to a formatted string, or changing semantic
meaning without versioning can break readers even if the producer code runs. During migrations,
dual-read/dual-write or versioned events may be safer than a sudden cutover. Schema validity is
also not full data quality: a syntactically valid status can still violate business rules. Treat
serialization/schema validation as one boundary, then apply domain validation and
quarantine/reconciliation as another.

Follow with me once

consumer with group.id=m14-shipment-a, auto.offset.reset=earliest and enable.auto.commit=False.
Validate JSON, write event IDs to a local idempotency ledger, and commit only after the durable
outcome. Stop with Ctrl-C so close() leaves the group cleanly.
from confluent_kafka import Producer
def delivered(err, msg):
if err:
print('FAILED', err)
else:
print(msg.topic(), msg.partition(), msg.offset())
p = Producer({'bootstrap.servers':'localhost:9092'})
p.produce('m14-orders', key='O17', value='{"event_id":"E17","status":"PAID"}', on_delivery=delivered)
p.flush()
What you should see
Producer output should report delivered topic/partition/offset. Consumer output should show
decoded key/value plus partition/offset, and a second run of the same group should resume after
committed work. A fresh group can replay retained records according to its reset policy.
Why it worked
The result follows from the contract just introduced rather than from a memorized command.
Preserve the evidence that proves the contract: keys/partitions/offsets, committed positions, sink
reconciliation, checkpoint state or lag by partition as appropriate.
Break it / common failure
Calling flush after every single event makes an asynchronous producer behave synchronously and
can destroy throughput; never flushing before process exit can leave queued events unsent. On the
consumer side, a busy loop with no error handling can hide broker/client problems.
Reason through a realistic incident
The script prints 'produced' before the callback reports an error. That is why enqueueing locally is not
delivery confirmation. Base evidence on callbacks/flush results and broker-side consumption, not a
print immediately after produce().
Deepen the engineering reasoning
The Python client workflow should make asynchronous behavior visible. Producer.produce()
generally enqueues work into the client; delivery callbacks are driven as the client services events,
and flush() is a shutdown/learning convenience rather than a throughput pattern to call after every
record. On the consumer side, poll() participates in both record delivery and group/client lifecycle.
The supplied route disables auto commit so the durability boundary is explicit. Each processed
record should save enough evidence to explain a restart: event_id, topic, partition, offset, durable
sink outcome and commit outcome. Invalid input should not disappear into console text. Persist a
quarantine record with raw payload and coordinates; once that quarantine outcome is durably
written, the lesson policy can treat the poison record as handled and commit past it. A production
system might instead retry with backoff, send to a dedicated DLQ topic, or stop the partition. The
important point is that the policy is explicit, observable and replayable, not accidental behavior
hidden inside an exception handler.

M14 lesson 11 of 12 | Primary practice: practice/kafka/11_* and simulator evidence where supplied
Why this matters
M12 taught Spark and M14 taught Kafka. This lesson joins them without pretending Kafka and Spark
are the same system. Kafka is the durable event log; Spark Structured Streaming is a compute
engine that reads partitions, tracks query progress/checkpoints and incrementally transforms data.
Picture it in your head
Kafka is the railway carrying numbered carriages. Spark Structured Streaming is a long-running
sorting facility beside the track. It repeatedly reads a range of Kafka offsets, transforms records, and
records its own checkpoint so the query can recover.

Follow with me once

key/value from bytes to strings, parse JSON, filter invalid amounts and write a console sink with a
checkpoint directory. Inspect topic, partition and offset columns. Stop/restart with the same

applying startingOffsets again.

--packages org.apache.spark:spark-sql-kafka-0-10_2.13:4.2.0 \
practice/kafka/11_spark_structured_streaming.py
What you should see
The streaming DataFrame schema includes Kafka metadata. Valid events appear after parsing. The
checkpoint directory is created after the query starts. Restart behavior follows checkpoint state when
it exists.
Why it worked
The result follows from the contract just introduced rather than from a memorized command.
Preserve the evidence that proves the contract: keys/partitions/offsets, committed positions, sink
reconciliation, checkpoint state or lag by partition as appropriate.
Break it / common failure
Do not confuse a Kafka consumer group's committed offsets with Spark Structured Streaming
checkpoint semantics. Spark's Kafka source manages its query progress through Spark
checkpointing; the integration docs explicitly describe Kafka-specific configuration boundaries.
Reason through a realistic incident
An engineer deletes the Spark checkpoint to 'fix' a stuck query and the pipeline reprocesses old
offsets into a non-idempotent sink. The checkpoint was part of correctness, not disposable cache.
Recovery should diagnose source offsets, query state and sink idempotency before destructive
reset.
Deepen the engineering reasoning
Spark Structured Streaming adds another state/progress layer on top of Kafka. Kafka still owns topic
partitions and offsets. Spark uses those offsets as source progress while its checkpoint directory
persists query metadata and state needed for recovery. Therefore startingOffsets is mainly a starting
rule for a new query without usable prior checkpoint state; an established query normally resumes
from checkpoint information. Deleting the checkpoint is not 'clear cache.' It changes the recovery
identity and can cause rereads, lost state or different semantics depending on the query and sink.
The checkpoint must live on durable storage appropriate to the environment, not a disposable path if
the query is production-critical. Kafka partition count also influences source parallelism, while Spark
can add downstream shuffle partitions for transformations. Keep those two kinds of partitioning
conceptually separate. In this course the console sink is learning evidence only. For durable targets,
design idempotent writes and save query progress, source offsets and output counts so restart
behavior can be demonstrated rather than guessed.

aggregate by status -> Delta sink. State the source key, checkpoint location and replay-safe sink
assumption.

window.

on.

pipeline reliable.

mastery.

checkpoints its own query state. Treat checkpoints and sink semantics as correctness controls.

Why tolerant conversion matters in Spark 4

ANSI behavior can make a normal cast of abc or NaN into a decimal raise an exception before quarantine can be written. The supplied classifier uses try_cast to obtain null for an invalid number, then assigns a reason. It also rejects negative amounts, excessive precision and unknown status. 12.50 / PAID is valid; abc is nonnumeric; -1 is negative; 1.234 violates the two-decimal contract. Decimal conversion alone could round 1.234 to 1.23, so the format check remains necessary. The two output writes in foreachBatch are not one transaction. The retry replaces only that micro-batch’s own paths. Read them only after the query batch succeeds. Never delete the checkpoint while reusing those output directories: the batch IDs can restart. This teaching sink does not demonstrate a general exactly-once multi-table transaction.

Why this matters
A streaming pipeline is not finished when messages flow once. Operations means knowing whether
it is keeping up, whether one partition is unhealthy, whether rebalances are normal, and how to
recover without hiding loss or duplication.
Picture it in your head
Producer progress is the front of a moving queue; consumer committed progress is a runner behind
it. Lag is the distance. A little distance can be normal. A distance that grows continuously means the
consumer cannot keep pace, is blocked, or is failing/rebalancing.

Break it / common failure
Lag=0 is not automatically healthy if no events are arriving, and nonzero lag is not automatically an
incident. Alerts need business freshness SLOs and trend/rate context. Another failure is sending
poison records to a DLQ and never operating the DLQ.
Reason through a realistic incident
Lag spikes after a deployment. Errors are low but rebalances occur every minute. Check whether
consumers are missing heartbeat/poll requirements because processing blocks too long. A scaling
change can make things worse if it increases rebalance churn without adding useful partition
parallelism.
Deepen the engineering reasoning
Lag is a symptom, not a diagnosis. Compute it per partition and look at the shape. One partition
falling behind while others are healthy suggests skew, a hot key, a poison or expensive record,
partition-specific broker/network trouble, or sink behavior tied to that data. All partitions rising
together after a deployment suggests a broader processing or downstream regression. Frequent
rebalances add another clue: consumers may be exceeding poll/processing expectations, crashing,
or changing membership too often. Build an incident sequence: confirm producer/log-end movement,
measure committed positions and lag, inspect assignments/rebalances, measure processing
latency, inspect sink latency/errors, then change one thing. Scale consumers only if partitions and
downstream capacity can use the extra workers. Validate recovery by watching lag trend return
toward a stable level while business reconciliation remains correct. A consumer catching up quickly
but dropping records incorrectly is not a successful recovery. Operations closes the loop between
Kafka metrics and the data-quality/reconciliation habits from earlier modules.

Validation and recovery ladder
•  First prove the broker/source is reachable before changing application logic.
•  Name the topic, partition, key/group/query identity and the exact progress marker you are relying
on.
•  Reconcile input evidence against valid output + quarantine/error outcomes; do not use a green
process as proof of correctness.
•  If a failure can cause replay, prove the sink or side effect handles replay safely before you call the
pipeline reliable.
•  Keep the genuine first attempt/error. A corrected run is repair evidence; the changed retry proves
mastery.
Ready-made revision
Operate streaming systems per partition and per business freshness objective. Lag is a symptom
that needs context, not a diagnosis by itself.
Evidence / mastery
Save: command or code used, one expected output, one failure/recovery note, and one sentence
explaining the guarantee/boundary in your own words. You are ready only when you can solve the
changed retry with the review closed.
